title: How to search for a file in Finder on Mac: steps, shortcuts and fixes
metaTitle: How to Search for a File in Finder on Mac (Step by Step)
description: Learn how to search for a file in Finder on Mac using the search field, Spotlight shortcuts, criteria, Smart Folders and fixes for missing files.
targetKeyword: how to search for a file in finder on mac
secondaryKeywords: search for a file in Finder Mac
intro: Open a Finder window, click the search field, type part of the file name and press Return. Finder lists the matches, and you can narrow them with criteria such as Kind, Date Modified or keywords like kind:images.
tldr: Open a Finder window from the Dock, type a file name or word in the search field, and press Return.
Press ⌥⌘Space to open a Finder window with the search field already selected.
Click Add below the search field to narrow results by Kind, Name, dates or Other.
Hold Option and click More to choose Any, All or None of your criteria.
If a file is missing from results, check Recents and Apple menu > Recent Items, then check Spotlight privacy.

blocks.text: How to search from the Finder window
Finder search sits in the window itself. Click the Finder icon in the Dock to open a Finder window. Then enter your search term in the search field and press Return. That is the whole basic search.

You do not need the exact name. Part of a name works. If you remember the file was called something like Q3 budget, type budget or q3. Scan the results for the folder and the date, because two files can share a name.
Which search starting point to use

rows: You want a Finder window with the search field already selected
You want a quick search that can also open apps and actions
The file was opened or changed recently
Apple's table calls it Find items in a document or open a Find window
You are in a text-editing context, which is not Finder file search
blocks.caption: Shortcuts as listed on Apple's Mac keyboard shortcuts page.

blocks.text: Spotlight and Finder search overlap, but they are not the same thing. Spotlight is the fast jump. Press ⌘Space, type a few letters and press Return to open the top result. Apple's Spotlight page says Command-R opens a result in its app or in Finder, which lets you move from one to the other.
Keyboard shortcuts for searching files

items: ⌥⌘Space opens a Finder window with the search field selected, so you can type right away.
⌘Space opens or closes Spotlight. Return opens the selected result.
⌘1 to ⌘4 narrow Spotlight results by category: Applications, Files, Actions and Clipboard.
⌘R opens a Spotlight result in its app or in Finder.
⇧⌘F opens the Recents window, which lists files you viewed or changed recently.
The slash key filters Spotlight results, according to Apple's Spotlight page.

blocks.title: Do not use ⌥⌘F for file search
blocks.text: Apple's shortcut table lists ⌥⌘F under text editing, as Go to the search field. It does not open Finder's file search. Use ⌥⌘Space for that.

⌘F is the shortcut most people try first. Apple's table describes it as Find items in a document or open a Find window, which is a general command. Test it in your Finder window. If it does not search files, use ⌥⌘Space.
How to narrow Finder search results
A broad search can return too many matches. Narrowing fixes that. Click Add on the right side of the search window, below the search field. The new row starts with a pop-up menu on the far left.

Choose a criterion from that far-left pop-up. Apple lists Kind, Name, Last Opened, Date Created and Date Modified. Choose Other to see more attributes. Then use the next pop-ups to set the value, such as a type of file or a date.

Here is a worked example. You remember a spreadsheet you edited last month, but not its name. Choose Kind and pick spreadsheets. Click Add again, choose Date Modified and set the date. Each row cuts the list down.

items: Click Add to start a new row of criteria under the search field.
Click Remove on a row to delete that criterion. Apple describes Add and Remove buttons for this.
Read the results after each change, so you know which row removed the match.
Remember that every criterion must match by default. Two strict rows can leave you with no results.

blocks.text: Any, All or None: match more than one rule

By default, a file must match all of your criteria. Sometimes you need a looser rule. Hold Option, then click the More button that appears. Choose whether Any, All or None of the criteria must be met.

Use Any for either-or searches. Say you want every PDF and every image in one list. Set the match to Any, then add Kind: PDF and Kind: Images. Use None to hide a type. None with Kind: Movies removes movies from the results. Hold Option each time, because More stays hidden without it.
Keyword search syntax in Finder

Typing is faster than clicking pop-ups once you know the keywords. Type a keyword, a colon, then the value. Apple's examples are kind:images and created:8/16/24. Apple also lists from, to, author, with, by, tag, title, name, keyword and contains.

rows: Files modified on or before July 29, 2024
Matches without the word invoice, because a minus sign means AND NOT
blocks.caption: Examples from Apple's Narrow your search results page. Dates use the month/day/year format in Apple's examples.

blocks.text: How to save a Finder search as a Smart Folder
Some searches come back every week, such as all invoices from this year. Do not rebuild them each time. Click Save below the search field. Apple says the search is saved as a Smart Folder.

Select Add To Sidebar to keep the Smart Folder one click away. A Smart Folder stores the rules, not a fixed list of files. Files that match the rules later show up when you open it. Name it after the rule, so you can find it again.
How to find a file you used recently

If you cannot remember the name, search by time instead. Click Recents in the Finder sidebar. Apple's troubleshooting steps say to use the Group control and choose Date Last Opened. The list then groups files by when you last opened them.
The Apple menu also has Recent Items. Choose Apple menu > Recent Items to see recent apps and documents. Use it when you opened the file from another app and never touched Finder.
Why a file does not show up in Finder search
Spotlight keeps an index of what is on your disks. If a file is missing from that index, search can miss it, even when the file is there. Three causes cover most misses.

First, the folder may sit on Spotlight's privacy list, which makes Spotlight skip it. Second, a file may have permissions that block your account. Third, you may be looking in iCloud. iCloud.com search is a different tool. It matches iCloud Drive file names, folder names and document types. It does not search files that exist only on your Mac.
How to rebuild the Spotlight index on Mac

Apple's fix is to add the disk or folder to Spotlight privacy, then remove it, so Spotlight indexes it again. Open Apple menu > System Settings > Spotlight. Some macOS versions call it Siri & Spotlight. Click Search Privacy or Spotlight Privacy at the bottom.

Click the plus button, or drag the folder in. Wait a few seconds. Select the folder in the list, click the minus button, click Done and quit System Settings. Then search again for a file you know is inside.

blocks.title: Permissions error
blocks.text: If you see an unknown or permissions error during this fix, your account may lack ownership of some items. Apple's rebuild article links to a guide on changing those permissions.
Mistakes people make with Finder search

items: Typing in Spotlight when you wanted the Finder search field. Press ⌥⌘Space for the Finder window instead.
Pressing ⌥⌘F and expecting a file search. Apple lists it as a text-field shortcut.
Forgetting Option before clicking More. Without Option, you cannot switch to Any, All or None.
Stacking criteria until nothing matches. Remove rows one at a time to find the one that blocks the file.
Adding a folder to Spotlight privacy and forgetting it. Spotlight skips anything on that list.
Assuming iCloud.com search covers files that exist only on your Mac. It does not.

blocks.text: Which macOS version these steps cover

Apple's current Mac User Guide pages for search are labeled macOS 27 Golden Gate in the version selector. Those pages do not say which versions the steps were tested on, so check your own menus. Menu names change between releases. Apple uses both Spotlight and Siri & Spotlight, and both Search Privacy and Spotlight Privacy.
Some people on macOS 26 report that Spotlight missed files Finder found. Those reports are anecdotal. Apple's pages do not address them, so test a file you know exists before you trust either search.
Where to go next

If you sort files by topic, tags make them easier to find. Read [how to add a tag to a file in Finder on Mac](/how-to/add-a-tag-to-a-file-in-finder). To keep your most used folders close, see [how to change the sidebar in Finder on Mac](/how-to/change-the-sidebar-in-finder).

If you want the path visible while you browse results, see [how to show the path bar in Finder on Mac](/how-to/show-the-path-bar-in-finder). Hidden files need a separate step, covered in [how to show hidden files in Finder on Mac](/how-to/show-hidden-files-in-finder).

faq.question: Why can't I find a file I know is on my Mac?
faq.answer: Check the spelling first, then try a shorter or more distinctive word. If it still misses, check Recents and Apple menu > Recent Items. If the file is still missing, its folder may be on the Spotlight privacy list.

faq.question: What is the shortcut to search in Finder?
faq.answer: Press ⌥⌘Space to open a Finder window with the search field selected. ⌘Space opens Spotlight, which is a separate search that can also open apps and actions.

faq.question: Does ⌘F search files in Finder?
faq.answer: Apple's shortcut table describes ⌘F as Find items in a document or open a Find window. Test it in your Finder window. For file search, use ⌥⌘Space, which opens Finder's search field.

faq.question: Can I search by date in Finder?
faq.answer: Yes. Click Add, choose Date Created or Date Modified, then set the date. You can also type a keyword such as modified:<=7/29/24, using the format in Apple's example.

faq.question: How do I find files with a specific tag?
faq.answer: Apple lists tag among its search keywords, so type tag: followed by the tag name. Check the results on your Mac to confirm the format works for your tags.

faq.question: Does iCloud.com search find files that are only on my Mac?
faq.answer: No. According to Apple, iCloud.com search matches iCloud Drive file names, folder names and document types. It does not search files that exist only on your Mac.

task: Find a file in Finder on Mac
appliesTo: Finder on macOS, following Apple's Mac User Guide search steps
requirements: A Mac running macOS, with Finder open or in the Dock.
Permission to change Spotlight privacy settings, only if you use the rebuild fix.
The file must be on this Mac or in a folder Spotlight indexes.

steps.name: Open a Finder window
steps.text: Click the Finder icon in the Dock. A Finder window opens. Or press ⌥⌘Space to open a Finder window with the search field already selected.
steps.tip: If the shortcut does nothing, click the Finder icon in the Dock instead.

steps.name: Click the search field
steps.text: Find the search field in the Finder window toolbar. Click it if it is not already active. After ⌥⌘Space, the field is already selected, so skip this step.
steps.tip: A blinking cursor in the field means it is ready for typing.

steps.name: Type a file name or word
steps.text: Type part of the file name, or a word you remember from it. You do not need the full name. A distinctive word returns fewer unrelated results.
steps.tip: Start with the most distinctive word, then add more only if you get too many results.

steps.name: Press Return
steps.text: Press Return to run the search. Apple's steps say to enter your search term and press Return. The matching files appear in the window.
steps.tip: If the list looks wrong, check the spelling first.

steps.name: Click Add to narrow results
steps.text: Click Add on the right side of the search window, below the search field. A row of criteria appears under the search field.
steps.tip: Click Add again to stack another criterion. Each row narrows the list.

steps.name: Choose a criterion
steps.text: Open the pop-up menu on the far left of the new row. Choose Kind, Name, Last Opened, Date Created or Date Modified. Choose Other to see more attributes.
steps.tip: Kind is the fastest way to limit results to images, PDFs or spreadsheets.

steps.name: Set the value
steps.text: Use the other pop-ups in the row to set the value. For Kind, pick a file type. For a date, pick the date you need.
steps.tip: Check the list after each change, so you know which row removed the match.

steps.name: Use keywords when you type fast
steps.text: Type a keyword, a colon and a value in the search field, such as kind:images. Put a minus sign before a term to exclude it, because the minus sign means AND NOT.
steps.tip: Dates in keywords follow the month/day/year format in Apple's example.

steps.name: Save the search if you repeat it
steps.text: Click Save below the search field. Apple says the search is saved as a Smart Folder. Select Add To Sidebar to show it in the sidebar.
steps.tip: Name the Smart Folder after its rule, so you can find it later.

shortcuts.action: Open a Finder window with search selected
Open a Spotlight result in its app or Finder
Open Recents, recently viewed or changed files
Find items in a document or open a Find window
Go to search field in text editing (not Finder search)

troubleshooting.problem: Spotlight misses a file you know exists
troubleshooting.fix: Add the folder to Spotlight privacy, wait a few seconds, then remove it. Open Apple menu > System Settings > Spotlight, then click Search Privacy or Spotlight Privacy.

troubleshooting.problem: The rebuild shows an unknown or permissions error
troubleshooting.fix: Your account may lack ownership of some items. Apple's rebuild article links to a guide on changing permissions. Fix that first, then rebuild the index.

troubleshooting.problem: A recent file is missing from Finder results
troubleshooting.fix: Open Recents, set the Group control to Date Last Opened, and look there. You can also open Apple menu > Recent Items.
Check which shortcut you pressed. ⌥⌘F goes to a text search field, not to Finder search. Use ⌥⌘Space or click the Finder icon in the Dock.

troubleshooting.problem: No results after you add criteria
troubleshooting.fix: Remove criteria one at a time with Remove until results return. The last row you removed holds the rule that blocked the file.

troubleshooting.problem: The Any, All or None option does not appear
troubleshooting.fix: Hold Option, then click More. The More button appears only while you hold Option.
